vignette: Layla was standing near the edge of the central plaza when the first detonation tore through the afternoon air. The shockwave threw her against a stone kiosk, and the world dissolved into a haze of dust and shattering glass. Before she could even draw a breath, a second blast rippled through the crowd, followed immediately by the sharp crack of gunfire. She scrambled on her hands and knees through the debris, her vision swimming as uniformed officers pushed through the panic, their heavy boots and drawn weapons filling the space. Above, the rhythmic thump of military helicopters cut through the sirens, a mechanical drumbeat that vibrated in her chest. She had spent the next hour curled beneath an overturned cart while men in tactical gear swept the area, their flashlights and authoritative commands echoing off the concrete. When they finally escorted her to a staging zone, she felt the full weight of what had just happened settle into her bones. In the months that followed, Layla found her nervous system fixed on a single frequency of threat. She stopped taking the subway route that ran past the plaza, but more than that, she began to flinch whenever a police cruiser slowed down on her suburban street. The sight of uniformed officers in any context, even a casual traffic stop, sent her pulse racing until her hands went numb. She could not sit through movies or news segments that showed violence, and she found herself stepping across the street whenever a physical altercation erupted between strangers. The hardest part was the sky. Whenever she heard the low whine of an aircraft or the heavy thud of a helicopter overhead, her breath would catch and her shoulders would lock. She had come to believe that the air itself had turned hostile, a conviction that made standing on her balcony unbearable. Over time, she stopped looking out the window, drawing the blinds shut early every afternoon. The changes in her life were slow and quiet until she noticed them all at once. She used to be a happy person who laughed easily at her husband’s dry jokes and lit up during weekend farmers market trips, but now she was always miserable. The color had drained from her days, leaving behind a flat, heavy stillness. When her husband asked what was wrong, she could not explain that she felt like she didn’t know herself anymore. The woman who had built a career managing complex projects and who had once trusted her own instincts was gone, replaced by someone who moved through rooms like a ghost, constantly scanning for exits. What frightened her most was the sense of being exposed. She was certain that others could see what happened to her just by looking at her, that her widened eyes and rigid posture broadcast her ruin to everyone around her. This awareness made eye contact feel like a physical weight. At work, the isolation grew thickest. As a project manager overseeing a commercial development downtown, she had to walk the active construction sites weekly. During a morning inspection last month, a police patrol drove slowly past the chain-link fence, and the sharp bark of a radio transmission crackled through the morning air. Layla froze on the scaffold, her clipboard slipping from her fingers. She had spent the previous night dreading the site visit, but the reality of standing there while the world operated normally felt impossible. She requested a transfer to remote coordination, a move that cost her professional standing and left her colleagues puzzled. Her marriage, once anchored by shared plans and easy conversation, now revolved around her need for predictability. She finally booked an appointment not because the fear had lessened, but because she was terrified of losing the last fragments of control she had left. She hoped someone might help her untangle the knot in her chest, even as she braced for the possibility that the therapist would see her exactly as she feared: completely laid bare.
